title: What Happens When You Lose Your Voice?
sources: NHS, 'Laryngitis' ('Laryngitis is when your voice box or vocal cords in the throat become irritated or swollen'; symptoms: hoarse voice, sometimes losing your voice; 'usually happens when you have an infection from a virus, such as cold or flu', also constant throat clearing, long-lasting coughing; usually goes away within 1 to 2 weeks; 'try to speak as little as possible'; 'do not talk loudly or whisper – both strain your voice'; drink plenty of fluids; see a GP if symptoms do not improve after 2 weeks or keep coming back; 111 if very painful or hard to swallow, 999 for difficulty breathing): https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/laryngitis/

Cleveland Clinic, 'Laryngitis' (inflammation of the larynx/voice box; 'swelling and inflammation affect how your vocal cords vibrate. They distort the sounds your vocal cords make, so your voice sounds weak or hoarse'; causes include common cold viruses and 'Overuse injuries or trauma (like overusing your voice, screaming, yelling or singing)', e.g. cheering 'at a concert or sports event'; 'Let your voice rest as much as you can'; 'Don't whisper, as even that can aggravate your symptoms'; acute symptoms last three to seven days, more than three weeks = chronic; talk to a provider if it lasts longer than a week or two): https://my.clevelandclinic.org/health/diseases/22268-laryngitis

Cleveland Clinic, 'Vocal Cords' ('Your vocal cords are two bands of muscle inside your voice box'; 'Your vocal cords may vibrate hundreds of times per second'; vocal cords come together for whispering, and spending too much time whispering can strain them): https://my.clevelandclinic.org/health/body/24456-vocal-cords

lines.text: What happens when you lose your voice?
To save it, should you whisper, or barely talk? Guess.

lines.text: So it's B: barely talk, and sip water.
Still hoarse after two weeks? See a doctor.
